source.title: Open problems in the theory of microwave heating

accepted.question_text: Consider the nonlinear microwave-heating initial-boundary value problem that couples Maxwell's equations for the electric and magnetic fields E(x,t), H(x,t) with a heat equation for the temperature θ(x,t) on a bounded simply connected domain Ω, where the electrical conductivity σ(θ) and the microwave energy absorption q(θ) both depend on θ. Assume σ(θ) > q(θ) for every temperature θ. Let M be the set of stationary data with E_0(x)=0 and H_0(x)=∇φ(x), where φ is harmonic in Ω. Must every regular solution satisfy lim_{t→∞} dist((E(t), H(t), θ(t)), M) = 0?
accepted.context_brief: Asymptotic convergence to the harmonic stationary set M

evidence.quote: (15) dV/dt = ∫_Ω [q(θ) − σ(θ)]|E|^2 dΩ. (16) σ(θ) > q(θ) for all θ.
If (16) holds, formula (15) suggests that (21). To prove (21) it appears natural to use the modern theory of dynamical systems [2].

accepted.question_text: For the full nonlinear microwave-heating problem coupling Maxwell's equations with the heat equation, where both the electrical conductivity σ(θ) and the thermal absorptivity q(θ) depend on the temperature, does the existence theory obtained by the Galerkin method together with the Schauder fixed point theorem actually give a unique solution?
accepted.context_brief: Uniqueness for the full Maxwell-heat system

evidence.quote: It is comparatively easy to prove that (1)–(9) has a solution using the Galerkin method (see [1]) coupled with the Schauder fixed point theorem. More difficult appears to prove that the solution is unique.

accepted.question_text: For the full nonlinear microwave-heating problem coupling Maxwell's equations with the heat equation, is the integral condition ∫_0^∞ dξ/q(ξ) = ∞ sufficient to guarantee that the solution exists for all time t ∈ [0,∞)?
accepted.context_brief: Global existence under the integral condition on q

evidence.quote: An additional difficulty is to establish under what assumptions this solution is defined in [0, ∞).
Remark In view of the above considerations it appears not unreasonable to presume that ∫_0^∞ 1/q(ξ) dξ = ∞ is the key assumption to prove that problem (1)–(9) has a solution defined in [0, ∞).
